title: Data Lifecycle: TTL, Archival & Tiered Storage
summary: Most data gets cheaper to store and less useful to query as it ages — designing for that curve instead of paying hot-storage prices for it forever.

slides.markdown:
Most data isn't equally valuable forever — a record accessed constantly in its first week is often barely touched a year later, yet many systems keep paying full hot-storage price for it regardless of age. **Data lifecycle management** — TTLs, tiered storage, archival, retention — designs deliberately for that decay instead of ignoring it.

This is a schema and architecture decision made up front, not a cleanup job someone writes after storage bills get too high.

slides.sectionTitle: Why data has a lifecycle: hot -> warm -> cold, and access patterns that justify moving it
slides.markdown:
Data usually moves through stages that mirror how often it's actually accessed. **Hot** data is read or written frequently and needs the fastest storage available — in-memory or fast SSD. **Warm** data is accessed occasionally — recent-but-not-current orders, last quarter's reports — and tolerates somewhat higher latency. **Cold** data is rarely or never read again except for compliance or audit — old logs, expired sessions, ancient invoices — and tolerates slow, cheap retrieval.

The justification for moving data between these tiers is simple: paying hot-storage prices for cold-access data is pure waste, and the access pattern (how often, how urgently) is the only signal that actually matters for the decision, not the data's age alone.

slides.sectionTitle: TTL expiry: deleting data automatically once it stops being useful
slides.markdown:
A **TTL** (time-to-live) attaches an expiration to a record — a session token, a cache entry, a verification code — so the system deletes it automatically once that time passes, with no manual cleanup job required. Many databases (DynamoDB, MongoDB, Redis) support TTLs natively as a field or setting on a collection, running expiry as a background process rather than an application-level cron job.

TTLs work best for data that's genuinely disposable — its value is time-boxed by design, like a password-reset link that must expire in 15 minutes. They're the wrong tool for anything that might need to exist longer under some circumstance, since a TTL deletes unconditionally once the clock runs out.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a record's path from primary store to warm tier to cold archive to deletion
slides.markdown:
![A record's lifecycle pipeline: primary store to warm tier at 30 days, to cold archive at 1 year, to deletion at 7 years, with decreasing storage cost and increasing retrieval latency at each stage](assets/lifecycle-pipeline.svg)

Each arrow in this pipeline is a policy decision, not an automatic side effect — someone decided 30 days, 1 year, and 7 years as the thresholds, presumably based on real access patterns and any compliance requirements.

Storage cost drops and retrieval latency rises at each stage, which is exactly the trade being made deliberately: data that's rarely read doesn't need to be instantly available.

slides.sectionTitle: Tiered storage: hot (SSD/in-memory) vs warm vs cold (object storage/archive) by cost and latency
slides.markdown:
| | Hot | Warm | Cold |
|---|---|---|---|
| Storage medium | In-memory / fast SSD | Standard SSD/HDD | Object storage archive tier (e.g. S3 Glacier) |
| Typical retrieval latency | Sub-millisecond to low ms | Tens of ms | Minutes to hours |
| Cost per GB | Highest | Moderate | Lowest |
| Good fit | Active sessions, current-quarter data | Recent-but-inactive records | Compliance archives, old backups |

The object store itself (see [object-and-blob-storage](object-and-blob-storage)) is often the physical home for both warm and cold tiers, distinguished by storage class rather than a different system entirely — moving a file to a cheaper storage class is usually a metadata change, not a data migration.

**How to decide:** measure actual access frequency by age, not guesses — if 90% of reads target the last 30 days, that's your hot/warm boundary, not an arbitrary round number.

slides.sectionTitle: Archival jobs: moving data out without an outage, and what stays queryable during the move
slides.markdown:
An **archival job** copies aging records from the primary store to a cheaper tier, then removes them from the primary store — usually run as a scheduled background batch rather than a one-time migration, since data keeps aging continuously. The job has to handle the same live-system constraints as any background migration: don't lock the table it's reading from, don't archive a record that's still being actively written to, and confirm the copy succeeded before deleting the original.

A common design decision is what stays queryable where: some systems keep archived data queryable through the same interface (a slower, unified query that checks cold storage when needed), while others require an explicit restore step before archived data can be queried at all — a trade between application simplicity and cost.

slides.sectionTitle: Compliance-driven retention: some data must be kept a minimum time, not just allowed to expire
slides.markdown:
Not every retention decision is about cost — some data must be **kept** for a minimum period by regulation (financial transaction records, healthcare data, certain audit logs), regardless of whether anyone ever queries it again. This flips the usual lifecycle question: instead of "when can we delete this to save money," it's "we're legally required to keep this even though it's cold and unread" — the answer is still tiered storage (cold, cheap), but never TTL-based deletion before the mandated period, and compliance requirements can also affect where that data is allowed to live geographically, a separate concern covered in data-residency-and-cross-region-cost.

Getting this wrong in either direction is costly: deleting too early risks legal or regulatory exposure; keeping everything hot forever "to be safe" burns money for no benefit once the access pattern has gone cold.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a TTL that deletes data a downstream system still silently depends on
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We set a 90-day TTL on this table to save storage — nothing reads data that old anyway."

**Why it's wrong:** "nothing reads it" is often an assumption, not a verified fact — a monthly reporting job, an annual reconciliation process, or a rarely-triggered support tool might depend on data past the TTL window, and the failure shows up months later as a silent gap or a confusing error, far removed from when the TTL was set.

**Correct model:** before setting a TTL, audit every consumer of the data — not just the obvious, frequent ones — and set the expiry to the longest genuine need, not the shortest guess. If any consumer's need is unclear, default to archiving to cold storage instead of deleting outright, since archival is reversible and outright deletion isn't.
